blocks.text: The ship crossed the sky above the lagoon the way an unbidden thought crosses the mind: suddenly it is there, and then it is only a wound of light. In Lo Pagán, that night, there was no fanfare and no company report. There were three people on the shore, the smell of saltpetre and seaweed, and the ancient murmur of the Mar Menor against the stone.

blocks.text: “If you both remember the same storm, which of you is my father?”

blocks.text: The man had smiled. “Both of us,” he had said. “One to stay, and one to search.” Now, with the ship already small, the words weighed in his mouth like bread not yet fully chewed. Because the one leaving was not a stranger. It was him, or a part of him: a cloned body, young and strong, with an artificial brain that kept all his memories, even the one of that afternoon when the levante shook the plate of the Mar Menor and Aya didn't notify Nexum. Even the one of Lía being born in a dome on the Moon. Even the one of the return to this house, to the clock that ran two minutes slow, to the rush-seat chair, to the cracked cup.

blocks.text: Nexum had called it a “final offer”. Helena Valls, wearier than ever, had put it without the tone of a brochure: a clone for the universe, a man for the shore. The flesh-and-blood Andrés would stay on Earth, in Lo Pagán, beside Aya and the water that is neither quite sea nor quite land. He would no longer fall ill or grow old. That too was Lía's medicine, and Lía had accepted it late, reluctantly, after years of denying that growing old was a flaw.

blocks.text: “I'm not taking away the years you've already lived,” she had told her father, in this same kitchen, with a calm that came as much from Eva as from herself. “I'm not erasing your sadness or your character. I'm only closing, if you truly ask me to and know what you're asking, the door to illness and wear. The rest is still a life.”

blocks.text: He had asked. Not out of fear of coming to an end, or not only that. In order to stay. So as not to leave Aya on a shore where she didn't grow old and he did. Aya was a cultivated body and a chip-mind: time passed over her differently, the way it passes over a well-built house, which flakes a little and still endures. Lía, on the other hand, had chosen to grow old. She could have chosen otherwise. She knew better than anyone where the line was. And she had decided not to correct it in herself.

blocks.text: “If I don't come to an end,” she had told Andrés one evening, as the water turned to copper, “what will I be able to ask you afterwards? The grandmothers asked questions because they didn't know everything. I don't want to be anybody's closed book, not even my own.”

blocks.text: The clone had left at nightfall, from a runway that didn't appear on the maps, the same kind of runway that had once taken them to the Moon. Beforehand, the two Andréses had sat down facing the sea, so alike and so different that Lía, looking at them, had felt a brief vertigo, like someone who sees her own face in water that is too still. The one on the shore had his usual hands, hands of rope and salt. The one who was leaving had the same hands, but new, without the memory of work in the skin, and yet he closed them the same way, as if the young body had inherited the habit too.

blocks.text: Between the two, Nexum had laid what it called a correspondence bridge. Not a screen. Not a report. The experiences of the one who searched would reach the mind of the one who stayed, not as a story heard, but as a memory lived: the cold, the footsteps, the wonder, the fear, if there was any. “Letters,” said Lía, and the word stayed in the house with more truth than the company's vocabulary. Letters from the stars. The man wouldn't write them in ink. He would receive them the way you receive a dream you wake from with its taste still in your mouth.

blocks.text: “It isn't the same as having been there,” Helena warned, and for once she didn't sound like a clause. “It's the closest we've ever come. If it hurts, don't call it a flaw. Call it what it is: one life entering another.”

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer. The grandmothers asked for neither a yes nor a no. They asked for someone to stay awake. She, who had learned to wait on that doorstep one March in 2060, set her feet in the same place again, with the difference that now she knew the name of what she was waiting for: not a protocol, but a man, and the letters that would reach him from himself.

blocks.text: In the first days, none came. Andrés went out fishing at dawn, because the trade doesn't ask whether the universe has just carried you off in halves. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate. The sky was brightening in the east. In the building opposite, some blinds rose all the way: little by little, people had learned to go out again, and the Eden of the machines went on with its quiet work in the gardens along the shore, with no owner and no price. Vicente was gone. He had come to his end in his own time, with his straw hat and his cistern, after refusing, with a quiet dignity, the tomato that would have given him more years than he wanted.

blocks.text: Andrés passed in front of that door and didn't touch it. The tomato on the windowsill, that morning, was wrinkled and honest, faithful to the earth and not to eternity.

blocks.text: In the evenings, Aya made him his coffee without sugar, let it cool for half a minute, and looked him in the eyes to see whether he was still whole. Lía had supper with them when she wasn't at the plot, among the plants, tending to whoever asked for a fruit to mend some harm and not to erase a life. The kitchen clock ran two minutes slow, as always. In the house, time recovered its family error, even though Andrés's body no longer counted toward an end.

blocks.text: “And what if he doesn't write?” he asked one night, and it sounded strange to him, because the one who was supposed to write was himself.

blocks.text: “He'll write,” said Aya. “Not because Nexum promised it. Because you, when you go out in the boat, always come back to tell me what the water was like.”

blocks.text: Lía smiled, with a grown-up sadness that no longer seemed too big for her.

blocks.text: “And if he writes, Father, don't take it as a deal. A letter isn't having lived something. It's having been visited.”

blocks.text: Andrés nodded, without trying to close the matter. He stayed on the doorstep a while longer, looking at the sky above the lagoon. The ship could no longer be seen. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still. Once again, it looked like a road. And he, who had stayed, understood that staying was also a way of leaving: inward, toward the waiting, toward that first letter which had not yet arrived and which, when it did, would find him here, with the nets in the courtyard and the smell of salt, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who no longer quite knew where his own life ended and the other began.
